title: Sorry, to Someone Who Won't Remember

pages.text:
Seventy-nine. I found Gus in the garage, curled up under a pile of moving blankets that looked like a green marshmallow left out in the rain. I sat down next to him, and for once I didn't roar or make a joke; I just looked at his spiky tail, which was tangled in the fabric.

"I'm sorry," I said. My voice sounded rusty, like a gate that hadn't been opened in weeks. "I told you it was just a costume. It's not. It's the bravest thing I know."

Gus lifted his head. His eyes were huge behind the plastic eyes of the T. rex hood. He didn't say anything. Instead, he reached into the pile and pulled out the spare tail he had been hiding. He held it out to me with both hands.

I took it. It was stiff and plastic and smelled like old carpet. I tucked it inside my red hoodie, against my back. It felt heavy, and it felt right. For the rest of the loops, I wore it. Not because it fixed anything. But because I needed to carry the thing that made him feel safe, even if he forgot he had given it to me.
pages.image: Gus, a small child in a green T. rex costume, sits in a garage under a pile of blankets, handing a plastic spiky tail to Max, an 11-year-old boy in a faded red hoodie who is kneeling on the concrete floor.

pages.text:
Eighty-two. Dusk. The yard grass was dead brown, brittle enough to snap if you stepped on it wrong. Dad sat on the curb with his knees pulled up to his chest. He looked smaller than usual, missing the bulk of the man who fanned smoke alarms, and instead had the posture of someone staring at a math worksheet they couldn't solve.

I sat down next to him. The concrete was cold through my jeans, a sharp, uncomfortable chill that made my toes curl.

"Are you scared?" I asked. I didn't ask about the job or Tucson. I just wanted to know if he was afraid.

He looked at me. His mustache twitched. He didn't make a pun, which was new. "Yeah," he said. "I think I am. I think it's too big for me."

I nodded and looked at the dead grass. "Your puns are the best part of the day," I said.

He stared at me. His face tightened, the muscles around his eyes pulling in until they looked like crumpled paper. "Even the toast one?"

"Especially the toast one."

He didn't say anything for a long time. Then he moved his arm around my shoulders and pulled me in. He hugged like a bear, which is what he was, but softer this time. I let him hold me. I didn't pull away.
pages.image: Dad, a large man with a dark mustache, sits on a concrete curb at dusk, hugging Max, an 11-year-old boy in a red hoodie, around the shoulders; dead brown grass surrounds them, and the sky is turning purple.

pages.text:
Eighty-four. Mom stood in the kitchen, perched on the edge of her stool with the clipboard clutched against her chest like a shield. Her thumb hovered over the last line on page six, the one she called the worries page.

"Read them," I said. I didn't raise my voice. I just wanted to hear what was heavy.

She froze, her pencil suspended in mid-air. Her eyes were wet, but she didn't wipe them. Instead, she turned the board toward me, her hand trembling slightly.

"The doctor," she read, her voice thin as a paper cut. "The friends. And the 'Will I be okay?' question."

I listened. I didn't interrupt. The silence settled between us, thick and quiet, like the air in a library right before the librarian snaps her fingers.

"I'll help you carry three," I offered.

She blinked, looking confused. "Which three?"

"The doctor. The friends. The 'Will I be okay?' one."

A sound escaped her, half-laugh, half-sob, tangled up tight. She pressed her forehead against the paper, hiding her face, while her shoulders shook. I didn't reach out to hug her. I just stood there, holding the space open, letting her cry into the checklist.
pages.image: Mom, a woman with curly black hair and a pencil behind her ear, stands at a kitchen sink, pressing her face against a clipboard with six pages of writing; Max, an 11-year-old boy in a red hoodie, stands nearby with his hands in his pockets.

pages.text:
Eighty-eight. Tessa was on her bed, drumsticks tapping a rhythm on the mattress. She heard me come in, but she didn't stop.

"I said something awful," I said, stopping right at the door because my legs wouldn't go any further. "And you don't remember it, but I do."

The tapping stopped. The sticks went still in her hands. "I don't remember it," she said, her voice flat.

"I know."

The ticking of the clock in the hall seemed very loud, like a second hand dragging itself across a face full of dust.

"Then you're weirdly good at apologizing for things that haven't happened yet," she said. Her eyes searched my face, looking for a lie.

"It happened."

She looked at me for a long time, and I felt like I was standing in the middle of a spotlight that only she could see. Then she reached out her hand and hooked her pinky around mine, a habit from when we were little, before we got too old for it.

"Okay," she said. "Thanks for telling me."
pages.image: Tessa, a teenage girl with a purple streak in her hair and headphones around her neck, sits on a bed, hooking her pinky finger around Max's, an 11-year-old boy in a red hoodie, who is standing by the door; drumsticks rest on the bedspread.

pages.text:
It didn't matter that they would forget. That was the thing I finally understood. The words didn't stick to them, but they stuck to me. I had said them. I meant them. And that was enough.

I went to my room and opened the closet door. The pencil was already in my hand, ready to work. I looked at the eighty-eight scratches on the wood. They were just lines, but they were my lines, a tally of every single time I had been the worst version of myself. I picked up the pencil, but I didn't add another scratch. Instead, I wrote a sentence. I made the letters big and blocky, like the ones we had to write for the spelling bee in third grade.

SORRY COUNTS EVEN IF NOBODY KEEPS IT.

I looked at the words until they felt solid and real, like a brick in a wall I was building for myself. I closed the closet door and walked to the hallway. The clock was silent. Gerald was still. I took a deep breath, feeling the air fill my lungs. There was one goodbye I hadn't done properly. The one with a bike helmet.
pages.image: Max, an 11-year-old boy with messy dark hair, stands in a hallway, looking at a cuckoo clock on the wall; his hand holds a yellow pencil, and his expression is quiet and resolute.
